To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

AAV vectors with the endothelial cell targeting motif SIGYPLP show enhanced transduction of endothelial cells, but not of vascular smooth muscle cells, and that intracellular trafficking is altered by targeting of AAV vectors.
a peptide targeting endothelial cells can be genetically incorporated into AAV capsids, resulting in a modified vector with enhanced transduction of endothelial cells.

we have genetically incorporated a peptide into the capsid of adeno-associated virus (AAV) to target the virus to endothelial cells, and have shown that this targeting is independent of heparin sulfate proteoglycan, a known receptor for AAV.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing AAV vectors that are capable of transducing EC.
the design, construction and testing of AAV vectors that are targeted to human endothelial cells (HEC), which are a major target for gene therapy in cardiovascular disease.
the development of a new generation of AAV vectors that can be directed to human vascular EC in vitro and in vivo, and that may be useful for the treatment of vascular disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we genetically incorporated a peptide that targets endothelial cells into position I- 587 of adeno-associated virus capsids and showed that this modification enhances transduction of endothelial cells, but not of vascular smooth muscle cells.
we have genetically incorporated the peptide, SIGYPLP into position I- 587 of the AAV capsids, which targets endothelium.
we have genetically engineered the AAV capsid to target EC and that this targeting is independent of heparin binding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the peptide SIGYLP can be incorporated into the capsid of an AAV2 vector, and the modified vector can be used to efficiently and selectively target human vascular endothelial and brain capillary endothelial cells.
the incorporation of the peptide SIGYLP into position I- 587 of the capsid protein of AAV2 results in a modified AAV2 vector with enhanced transduction of endothelial cells (AAVsig).
we have developed a new AAV vector with enhanced tropism to EC and altered trafficking within EC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the targeting of AAV to EC can be achieved through the use of a short peptide.
the AAV2 capsid can be modified to alter its tropism to target specific cells, in this case endothelial cells.
the peptide SIGYLP, when incorporated into AAV, can be used to target AAV to EC, and this is a promising strategy to develop AAV vectors with improved tropism.
